lesson.title: First, Outer, Inner, Last: The FOIL Shortcut for Binomials
lesson.summary: FOIL is a memorable shortcut, First, Outer, Inner, Last, for multiplying two binomials, producing exactly four products to combine.
lesson.body:
A binomial is a polynomial with exactly two terms, and multiplying two binomials is one of the most frequent operations in algebra. You already know how to do this from multiplying polynomials in general: distribute every term of the first binomial across every term of the second. Because a binomial has only two terms, that process always produces exactly four products, 2 terms times 2 terms, and those four products have a memorable order. The acronym FOIL, First, Outer, Inner, Last, is simply a way to make sure you find all four without missing one.

First means multiply the first term of each binomial together. Outer means multiply the two terms on the outside of the expression when it is written next to itself. Inner means multiply the two terms in the middle. Last means multiply the second term of each binomial together. FOIL is not a new rule of algebra; it is a memory device for the same distributive process you already know, restricted to the case of two terms times two terms. A common error is to multiply only the First and Last terms and forget the Outer and Inner cross terms entirely; that mistake drops the entire middle term of the answer, so it is worth double checking that all four products are present before combining.

Try (2x + 5)(3x - 4). First: 2x times 3x is 6x^2. Outer: 2x times negative 4 is negative 8x. Inner: 5 times 3x is 15x. Last: 5 times negative 4 is negative 20. Adding all four products gives 6x^2 - 8x + 15x - 20. The two middle terms, negative 8x and 15x, are like terms and combine to 7x, so the simplified product is 6x^2 + 7x - 20.

Check the result by substituting x = 1. The original expression gives (2 + 5)(3 - 4) = 7 times negative 1, which is negative 7. The simplified answer gives 6 + 7 - 20, which is also negative 7. Since both sides agree, the multiplication is correct. A second check with x = 0 is even faster: the original gives 5 times negative 4, or negative 20, and the simplified answer gives 0 + 0 - 20, also negative 20, which is really just confirming that the constant term was copied correctly from the Last step.

FOIL also has a geometric meaning worth keeping in mind. If you imagine (2x + 5) and (3x - 4) as the two side lengths of a rectangle, splitting each side into its two pieces divides the rectangle into four smaller rectangles, one for each of First, Outer, Inner, and Last, and the total area equals the sum of those four smaller areas. This is the same reasoning behind the box or table method mentioned for general polynomial multiplication, just restricted to a two by two grid because each binomial has only two terms.

FOIL only works when you are multiplying two binomials; it says nothing about a binomial times a trinomial or larger. For those cases you fall back on the full distributive process from multiplying polynomials, term by term, with more than four products to track. What makes FOIL worth learning on its own is that certain binomial times binomial products follow such consistent patterns that you can skip the four separate steps entirely once you recognize the pattern, which is exactly the idea behind special products, covered next.
